subject: physics
title: Circuit symbols and measuring current and potential difference
key_idea: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols for each component. An ammeter measures current and is connected in series. A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel across the component.

blocks.text: A circuit diagram uses a standard symbol for each component, joined by straight lines for wires. This section covers the symbols you need to recognise and draw.

rows: One long line and one short line
Supplies energy to the circuit. The long line is the positive terminal.
Two or more cells joined end to end
Supplies energy. Cells in series add their potential differences.
A gap in the wire with a hinged contact
A rectangle with an arrow through it
Resistance can be changed by hand.
A circle with a cross inside
A circle with an M inside
A triangle pointing at a bar
Lets current pass in one direction only: the direction the triangle points.
A diode symbol in a circle with two arrows pointing away
A light emitting diode. Gives out light.
A rectangle with a bent line through it
A rectangle in a circle with two arrows pointing in
A circle with an A inside
A circle with a V inside

items: Draw wires as straight lines with no gaps, except where a switch is open.
Show the positive and negative terminals of a cell or power supply the right way round.
A d.c. circuit has a **closed loop** from one terminal of the supply to the other.
Learn the standard symbol for every component in the table.
The long line on a cell is the positive terminal.
A diode passes current one way. An LED is a diode that gives out light.

blocks.text: Two meters test a circuit. Each one is connected in a different way.

items.meaning: Measures the current, in amperes (A), in a component.
Measures the potential difference, in volts (V), across a component.

items: Connect the **ammeter** in series with the component. The current in the component goes through the ammeter.
Connect the **voltmeter** in parallel with the component. It is placed across the component, on its own branch.
Build the circuit first as one series loop. Then add the voltmeter across the component last.

diagram.alt: Sort each statement into ammeter or voltmeter.

items.text: Connected in series with the component
Connected in parallel with the component

items: Ammeter: in series, measures current in amperes.
Voltmeter: in parallel, measures potential difference in volts.
Name the meter by what it measures: ammeter for current, voltmeter for potential difference.

sections.heading: Using a circuit to test a component

blocks.text: A test circuit measures the current in a component and the potential difference across it. The same circuit works for a lamp or a fixed resistor.

items: Swap the lamp for the fixed resistor.
Measure the current for different potential differences.
Repeat the experiment to check the results.

blocks.text: A power supply with fixed settings only gives whole numbers of volts. A component added to the circuit can make the potential difference across the lamp change continuously.

items: Add a **variable resistor** in series with the lamp. Changing its resistance changes the current and the potential difference.
Or add a **potential divider** in parallel with the power supply.
To test a component, measure current and potential difference together.
A variable resistor in series gives a continuously variable potential difference.

checks.q: How is an ammeter connected to a component?
checks.a: In series with the component. It measures the current in the component.

checks.q: A student wants to measure the potential difference across a lamp. Name the meter and say how it is connected.
checks.a: A voltmeter, connected in parallel with (across) the lamp.

checks.q: A power supply only gives whole numbers of volts. Describe how to add a component so the potential difference across a lamp can be changed continuously.
checks.a: Add a variable resistor in series with the lamp (or in series with the power supply).

worked_example.question:
A student investigates how the current in a lamp changes with the potential difference across the lamp.

The student used a power supply that had fixed output voltage settings.
Each of these outputs was a whole number of volts.

Describe how the student could add a component to the circuit that would provide a continuously variable voltage across the lamp.
answer_points: Connect it in series with the lamp or the power supply.
Or add a potential divider (potentiometer), connected in parallel with the power supply.
worked_example.tip: Name the component for one mark and give its position for the second. The second mark depends on the first.

worked_example.question:
A student has written two sentences about the resistance of different electrical components.

The resistance of a filament lamp is so high in one direction, that no current can pass through.

The resistance of a thermistor changes as the light intensity changes.

The student has made two mistakes about the components.

Identify the mistakes and write the correct word or words to replace each of them.
answer_points: Mistake: thermistor. Correction: light dependent resistor (LDR).
Or the second mistake is light intensity. Correction: temperature.
worked_example.tip: Each mistake needs its correction. Light emitting diode or LED is allowed for diode.

worked_example.question:
A circuit contains a battery, a switch, a voltmeter and three 40 Ω resistors, R₁, R₂ and R₃. With the switch open, resistors R₁ and R₂ form a potential divider.

Describe what is meant by a potential divider.
answer_points: It splits (shares) the potential difference of the power source between two resistors or components connected in series.
The potential difference is shared in proportion to the resistances.
worked_example.tip: Any two of these ideas earn the two marks.

extra.heading: More components and how they behave

blocks.text: These components also appear in circuit diagrams.

columns: How it behaves in the circuit
rows: Gives a potential difference to the circuit. A d.c. supply pushes current one way.
Transfers kinetic energy to electrical energy.
Transfers electrical energy as thermal energy.
Rings when a current flows through it.
Melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too large.
Becomes a magnet when a current flows in it.
A switch that is turned on by a small current in a coil. It switches a separate circuit.
Two coils that change the size of an alternating potential difference.

items: **Thermistor (NTC only):** its resistance falls as the temperature rises.
**LDR:** its resistance falls as the light intensity rises.
**Variable resistor:** moving the slider changes the resistance and so the current.

blocks.text: Meters can be analogue (a pointer on a scale) or digital (a number on a display). Many have more than one range.

items: Choose the range just above the largest current or potential difference you expect.
Read the scale that belongs to the range selected.
If the reading is very small on a large range, switch to a smaller range for a more precise reading.

blocks.text: (Supplement) A potential divider splits the potential difference of the supply between resistors in series, in proportion to their resistances.
(Supplement) A variable potential divider lets the output potential difference be changed. Change the resistance of one resistor, for example with a variable resistor, an LDR or a thermistor.

worked_example.question:
A student replaces a filament lamp in a circuit with a light emitting diode (LED). The student also replaces the cell with an alternating current (a.c.) power supply.

Explain why the LED flashes on and off in this circuit.
answer_points: An LED only allows current in one direction, so it does not light when the current is reversed.
worked_example.tip: Any two of these ideas earn the two marks.

blocks.text: A lamp or an LED can be used as an indicator in a circuit.

items: If the lamp or LED lights, a current is flowing in that part of the circuit.
If it is off, there is no current in that part.
